content: Since 2005, the Chikungunya virus outbreak has been ongoing, with evidence suggesting that genetic mutations in the virus's coat protein have increased its ability to replicate in mosquito cells. This adaptation has allowed the virus to utilize the Asian tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus), an invasive species, as a vector in addition to its primary vector, Aedes aegypti. In July 2006, researchers identified specific genetic changes in the virus that contributed to the increased virulence of recent strains. In February 2005, an outbreak was reported on Réunion Island in the Indian Ocean, where by May 2006, 258,000 residents (out of a population of 777,000) had been infected, with 219 deaths officially attributed to the virus. Neighboring regions, including Mauritius, Madagascar, the Comoros, Mayotte, and the Seychelles, also reported cases. In India, the city of Nandurbar in Maharashtra experienced fatalities among individuals over 60 years old due to complications from Chikungunya. Patients continued to suffer from severe joint pain, dyspepsia, relapsing fever, and joint swelling months after infection. Physicians were advised to monitor for platelet abnormalities indicative of dengue or malaria. In 2006, a significant outbreak occurred in Andhra Pradesh, India, with initial cases reported in Hyderabad, Secunderabad, and Anantpur as early as late 2005. In Hyderabad alone, practitioners were seeing 10–20 cases daily. Some deaths were attributed to the misuse of antibiotics and anti-inflammatory drugs. Severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and loss of glycemic control were major contributors to morbidity. Recovery was typical, but 3–5% of cases experienced prolonged arthritis. The virus's ability to cause thrombocytopenia made the use of certain drugs risky, as they could lead to gastric erosion and upper gastrointestinal bleeding. The use of steroids for joint pain and inflammation was deemed dangerous and unwarranted. In Karnataka, India, at least 80,000 people across multiple districts were affected by December 2005. A separate outbreak in Malegaon, Maharashtra, in March 2006 resulted in over 2,000 cases. In Orissa, 5,000 cases of fever with muscle aches and headaches were reported between February and March 2006. By May 2006, Bangalore and neighboring Andhra Pradesh were experiencing outbreaks characterized by arthralgia, arthritis, and rashes. North Karnataka districts, including Gulbarga, Koppal, Bellary, Gadag, and Dharwad, were severely affected by late May 2006. Residents were urged to prevent water stagnation to reduce mosquito breeding grounds. In Tamil Nadu, India, 20,000 cases were reported in June 2006, with the virus spreading from the outskirts of Bangalore into the city. By July 2006, over 300,000 people in Karnataka were affected. In Chennai, fresh cases were reported, with southern districts like Kanyakumari and Tirunelveli heavily impacted. By August 2006, nearly 100,000 people in Tamil Nadu were infected, with Chennai being one of the worst-hit areas. The government’s claim of no deaths was questioned. Neighboring cities like Salem, Erode, and Coimbatore were also severely affected. In September 2006, outbreaks were reported in western India, particularly in southeast Gujarat, following heavy rains and floods. Cases were also noted in Goa, especially in South Goa, with 5,000 people affected. In Rajasthan, thousands of cases were detected in districts like Rajsamand, Bhilwara, Udaipur, and Chittorgarh after floods in August 2006, though these were not widely reported in the media. By September 2006, cases were spreading to northern India, with confirmed infections in Etawah and Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh. In September 2007, 130 cases were confirmed in Ravenna, Italy, specifically in the towns of Castiglione di Cervia and Castiglione di Ravenna, with one death reported. Symptoms included rash, fever, muscle and joint pain, and severe headache. Antihistamines were prescribed for itching, and patients were advised to rest and stay hydrated. Fatigue lasting six weeks often followed the acute illness phase. By October 2006, Kerala, India, reported 61 deaths and 30,000 hospital admissions due to Chikungunya, with additional cases treated in private clinics. In Tamil Nadu, the Andaman Islands, and other regions, the virus reached epidemic proportions, with relapsed cases presenting severe pain, swelling, vomiting, and general weakness.
